142	        a, b = self.fact(f"idx:{series}@{m1}"), self.fact(f"idx:{series}@{m2}")
143	        if not a or not b or not a.get("value"):
144	            return None
145	        pct = (b["value"] / a["value"] - 1) * 100
146	        if pct > -0.5:
147	            return None  # a rising driver confirms the supplier's case
148	        name = SERIES_NAME.get(series, f"The index {series}")
149	        return {
150	            "kind": "index",
151	            "ids": [f"idx:{series}@{m1}", f"idx:{series}@{m2}"],
152	            "text": f"{name} changed {pct:.1f}% from {m1} to {m2} (idx:{series}@{m1}, idx:{series}@{m2}).",
153	            "strength": 3 + min(3.0, abs(pct) / 3),
154	        }
155	
156	    def drivers(self, part):
157	        return [r["series_id"] for r in self.query("SELECT series_id FROM cost_drivers WHERE part_id = ?", (part,))]
158	
159	    def forecast(self, part):
160	        ids = self.ids(f"fc:{part.split(':')[-1]}@")
161	        f = self.fact(ids[-1]) if ids else None
162	        if not f or (f.get("change_pct") or 0) <= 0:
163	            return None
164	        text = f"Our forecast for this part is up {f['change_pct']:.1f}% ({ids[-1]})."
165	        return {"kind": "forecast", "ids": [ids[-1]], "text": text, "strength": 2}
166	
167	    def rival_quote(self, part, sid, price):
168	        """A quote of this case from another supplier, cheaper than this supplier's price."""
169	        out = []
170	        for ref in self.refs:
171	            f = self.fact(ref) if ref.startswith("quote:") else None
172	            if f and f.get("part") == part and f.get("supplier") != sid and price and f["unit_price"] < price:
173	                out.append(
174	                    {
175	                        "kind": "rival",
176	                        "ids": [ref],
177	                        "text": f"We hold another quote for this part at {money(f['unit_price'])} per unit ({ref}).",
178	                        "strength": 6,
179	                        "rival": True,
180	                    }
181	                )
182	        return out
183	
184	    def signal_notes(self, sid):
185	        """Its own words in our notes that weaken its case: material bought forward at fixed prices,
186	        an offer to open its calculation. Context for the person reading, not a checked figure."""
187	        out = []
188	        for d in self.query(
189	            "SELECT id, date, kind, file FROM documents WHERE supplier_id = ? ORDER BY date DESC", (sid,)
190	        ):
191	            path = self.pkg.root / (d.get("file") or "") if self.pkg else None
192	            text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") if path and path.is_file() else ""
193	            if re.search(r"covered at fixed prices|bought their \w+ forward|material covered until", text, re.I):
194	                out.append(
195	                    {
196	                        "kind": "hedged",
197	                        "ids": [d["id"]],
198	                        "text": f"Your letter of {d['date']} ({d['id']}) says your material is covered at fixed "
199	                        "prices, so recent index movements do not reach your costs yet.",
200	                        "strength": 5,
201	                    }
202	                )
203	            if re.search(r"walk us through their calculation", text, re.I):
204	                out.append(
205	                    {
206	                        "kind": "open_book",
207	                        "ids": [d["id"]],
208	                        "text": f"In our call of {d['date']} ({d['id']}) you offered to walk us through your "
209	                        "calculation; we would welcome that now.",
210	                        "strength": 4,
211	                    }
212	                )
213	        seen, uniq = set(), []
214	        for c in out:
215	            if c["kind"] not in seen:
216	                seen.add(c["kind"])
217	                uniq.append(c)
218	        return uniq
219	
220	    def currency(self, sid):
221	        """A supplier paying its costs in a currency that weakened against the euro earns more of it
222	        per euro: the ECB rate (its currency per euro) rose."""
223	        rows = self.query("SELECT country FROM suppliers WHERE id = ?", (sid,))
224	        cur = COUNTRY_CURRENCY.get(rows[0]["country"]) if rows else None  # it invoices in EUR, pays costs locally
225	        if not cur:
226	            return None
227	        ids = self.ids(f"idx:ECB-{cur}@")
228	        if not ids:
229	            return None
230	        m2 = ids[-1].split("@")[-1]
231	        m1 = months_back(m2, 12)
232	        a, b = self.fact(f"idx:ECB-{cur}@{m1}"), self.fact(f"idx:ECB-{cur}@{m2}")
233	        if not a or not b or not a.get("value"):
234	            return None
235	        pct = (b["value"] / a["value"] - 1) * 100
236	        if pct < 0.5:
237	            return None  # its currency got stronger: that argues its case
238	        refs = f"idx:ECB-{cur}@{m1}, idx:ECB-{cur}@{m2}"
239	        return {
240	            "kind": "currency",
241	            "ids": [f"idx:ECB-{cur}@{m1}", f"idx:ECB-{cur}@{m2}"],
242	            "text": f"The euro rose {pct:.1f}% against the {cur} from {m1} to {m2} ({refs}), so your costs "
243	            f"in {cur} take fewer euros.",
244	            "strength": 4 + min(3.0, pct / 3),
245	        }
246	
247	    def scorecard(self, sid, quality):
248	        ids = self.ids(f"sc:{sid.split(':')[-1]}@")
249	        if not ids:
250	            return None
251	        f = self.fact(ids[-1])
252	        if f is None:  # demo world: cite without a figure
253	            text = f"We have reviewed your delivery performance in our supplier scorecard ({ids[-1]})."
254	            return {"kind": "scorecard", "ids": [ids[-1]], "text": text, "strength": 2}
255	        if quality:
256	            if (f.get("ppm") or 0) < 1000:
257	                return None
258	            text = f"Your deliveries ran at {f['ppm']} ppm in {f['quarter']} ({ids[-1]})."
259	        else:
260	            if (f.get("otd_pct") or 100) >= 90:
261	                return None
262	            text = f"Your on-time delivery was {f['otd_pct']}% in {f['quarter']} ({ids[-1]})."
263	        return {"kind": "scorecard", "ids": [ids[-1]], "text": text, "strength": 2}
264	
265	    def demo_refs(self):
266	        """Refs the package cannot resolve: cited without a figure."""
267	        words = {
268	            "cost": ("should_cost", "Our bottom-up should-cost estimate for this part is on file ({ids}).", 5),
269	            "po": ("order_history", "We compared your offer with our recent order prices for this part ({ids}).", 4),
270	        }
271	        out = []
272	        for kind, (name, text, strength) in words.items():
273	            ids = [r for r in self.refs if r.startswith(f"{kind}:") and self.fact(r) is None]
274	            if ids:
275	                out.append(
276	                    {"kind": name, "ids": ids[:3], "text": text.format(ids=", ".join(ids[:3])), "strength": strength}
277	                )
278	        doc = self.case.get("trigger_doc")
279	        ctr = next((r for r in self.refs if r.startswith("ctr:")), None)
280	        if doc and ctr and self.fact(doc) is None and self.case.get("type") == "price_increase":
281	            text = f"Your letter ({doc}) gives less notice than our agreement provides for ({ctr})."
282	            out.append({"kind": "notice", "ids": [doc, ctr], "text": text, "strength": 5})
283	        return out
284	
285	    # -- per supplier ----------------------------------------------------------------------
286	    def for_supplier(self, sid, quote):
287	        """Every argument for this supplier that pushes our way, strongest first."""
288	        case, out = self.case, []
289	        quality = case.get("type") == "quality" or case["buyer"].get("category_goal") == "quality_first"
290	        single = len(case.get("parts") or []) == 1  # a bundle's price is not one part's order price
291	        for part in case.get("parts") or []:
292	            history = self.order_history(part, sid, quote) if single else None
293	            out += [c for c in (self.should_cost(part, sid, quote), history) if c]
294	            out += [c for c in (self.index_change(s) for s in self.drivers(part)) if c]
295	            out += self.rival_quote(part, sid, quote)
296	            if c := self.forecast(part):
297	                out.append(c)
298	        if c := self.notice(sid):
299	            out.append(c)
300	        out += self.signal_notes(sid)
301	        if c := self.currency(sid):
302	            out.append(c)
303	        if c := self.scorecard(sid, quality):
304	            out.append(c)
305	        if self.foreign:
306	            out += self.demo_refs()
307	        seen, uniq = set(), []
308	        for c in sorted(out, key=lambda c: -c["strength"]):
309	            if tuple(c["ids"]) not in seen:
310	                seen.add(tuple(c["ids"]))
311	                uniq.append(c)
312	        return uniq
313	
314	
315	def rival_offer(sid, offer_id, price):
316	    """Another bidder's standing offer in this session, citable to the others."""
317	    return {
318	        "kind": "rival",
319	        "ids": [offer_id],
320	        "text": f"Another bidder offers {money(price)} per unit for this part ({offer_id}).",
321	        "strength": 7,
322	        "rival": True,
323	        "from": sid,
324	    }

"""The model writes one paragraph of each e-mail: it answers the supplier's last e-mail like a
person would (its questions, its points, its situation). Code writes everything that binds or is
checked: figures, data IDs, the proposal. A paragraph with any digit, data ID or leak is dropped
and the template stands in. Hard timeout: the move goes out without the model if it is late."""

import logging
import os
import re
import time

import httpx

log = logging.getLogger("buyer")
TIMEOUT_S = 20.0
FORBIDDEN = re.compile(
    r"\d|\b(?:idx|quote|offer|sc|qn|po|cost|fc|news|doc|ctr):|urgent|urgency|deadline|budget|no alternative|"
    r"walk away|other options|last chance|desperate|must close|time pressure|target price",
    re.I,
)

SYSTEM = """You are a senior buyer at Hollerau Pumpenwerke, a German pump maker, writing to a supplier.
Write ONLY the middle paragraph of our reply e-mail: 2 to 4 sentences, plain text, no greeting, no
sign-off, no lists.

In it:
- answer the supplier's last e-mail like a thoughtful person: respond to what it asked and to the
  reasons it gave, using only the facts listed under WHAT WE CAN SAY;
- acknowledge its situation where the notes give one (for example cash needs, full capacity, rising
  costs, a long relationship), sincerely and briefly;
- if it asks for something we cannot give, say so kindly and point to what we do offer;
- ask one short question only if QUESTION ALLOWED is yes.

Never write any number, price, percentage, date, quantity or data ID (code adds the figures). Never
mention urgency, deadlines, a budget, our alternatives or the lack of them, a target price, or that
we will walk away. Never invent facts, promises or commitments. Be polite, factual and warm unless the
tone says firm."""


def complete_from_env():
    """(system, user) -> text with the team's OpenAI-compatible model, or None when not configured."""
    model, key = os.environ.get("LLM_MODEL"), os.environ.get("LLM_API_KEY")
    if not model or not key:
        return None
    base = os.environ.get("LLM_BASE_URL", "https://api.openai.com/v1").rstrip("/")
    client = httpx.Client(timeout=TIMEOUT_S, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"})

    effort = os.environ.get("LLM_EFFORT", "low")

    def complete(system, user):
        messages = [{"role": "system", "content": system}, {"role": "user", "content": user}]
        body = {"model": model, "messages": messages, "reasoning_effort": effort}
        r = client.post(f"{base}/chat/completions", json=body)
        r.raise_for_status()
        return r.json()["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]

    return complete


def paragraph(complete, brief):
    """The model's paragraph for this brief, or None (no model, late, broken or unsafe)."""
    if complete is None:
        return None
    t0 = time.monotonic()
    try:
        text = (complete(SYSTEM, brief) or "").strip()
    except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001 - a slow or broken model must not cost the move
        log.warning("writer model failed after %.1fs: %s", time.monotonic() - t0, e)
        return None
    text = " ".join(text.split())
    if not text or len(text) > 900 or FORBIDDEN.search(text):
        log.warning("writer paragraph dropped: %r", text[:200])
        return None
    log.info("writer paragraph in %.1fs", time.monotonic() - t0)
    return text

"""`buyer` command line: play one case or a whole set with our agent, and pull finished sessions
(result, trace with the supplier's reasons, back office) into logs/ for the learning loop."""

import argparse
import functools
import json
import logging
import os
import statistics
from pathlib import Path

from arena_kit import ArenaClient, ArenaError, RemoteTable, play, play_all
from arena_kit.cli import load_env, summary
from arena_kit.play import hosted, play_waves

from . import llm, runner
from .agent import AGENTS, load_package, naive_factory

LOGS = Path("logs/sessions")


def pull(client, set_):
    """Save every ended session of a set that has its trace to logs/sessions/<set>/, once."""
    out = LOGS / set_
    out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    saved = 0
    for s in client.sessions(set_):
        path = out / f"{s['case_id'].split(':')[-1]}_{s['session_id']}.json"
        if s["status"] != "ended" or path.exists():
            continue
        state = client.session(s["session_id"])
        if not (state.get("result") or {}).get("trace"):  # final: the trace comes after the final
            continue
        try:
            state["backoffice"] = client.backoffice(s["session_id"])
        except ArenaError:
            state["backoffice"] = None
        path.write_text(json.dumps(state, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False))
        saved += 1
    print(f"{saved} new sessions in {out}")


def main(argv=None):
    load_env()
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="buyer")
    ap.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true")
    verbose = argparse.ArgumentParser(add_help=False)  # -v also after the command
    verbose.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true", default=argparse.SUPPRESS)
    verbose.add_argument("--no-llm", action="store_true", default=argparse.SUPPRESS, help="template e-mails only")
    sub = ap.add_subparsers(dest="cmd", required=True)
    sub.add_parser = functools.partial(sub.add_parser, parents=[verbose])
    data = {"default": os.environ.get("ARENA_DATA"), "help": "data package folder"}
    p = sub.add_parser("play", help="play one case")
    p.add_argument("case_id")
    p.add_argument("--agent", default="buyer", choices=AGENTS)
    p.add_argument("--data", **data)
    r = sub.add_parser("run", help="play every playable case of a set in parallel; final: wave by wave")
    r.add_argument("--set", default="practice", choices=["practice", "sandbox", "final"])
    r.add_argument("--agent", default="buyer", choices=AGENTS)
    r.add_argument("--data", **data)
    r.add_argument("--parallel", type=int, default=8, help="cases at once (at most 10)")
    r.add_argument("--waves", type=int, default=5, help="final: stop after this many waves have closed")
    r.add_argument("--cases", help="practice or sandbox: only these cases, e.g. P01,P08")
    s = sub.add_parser("pull", help="save finished sessions with trace and back office to logs/sessions/")
    s.add_argument("--set", default="practice", choices=["practice", "sandbox", "final"])
    args = ap.parse_args(argv)
    args.no_llm = getattr(args, "no_llm", False)
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO if args.verbose else logging.WARNING,
        format="%(asctime)s %(message)s",
        datefmt="%H:%M:%S",
    )
    client = ArenaClient()

    if args.cmd == "pull":
        return pull(client, args.set)
    naive = args.agent == "naive"
    pkg = None if naive else load_package(args.data)
    complete = None if naive or args.no_llm else llm.complete_from_env()
    if args.cmd == "play":
        table = RemoteTable(client)
        try:
            if naive:
                result = play(table, args.case_id, naive_factory()())
            else:
                result = runner.play_case(table, args.case_id, pkg, complete=complete)
        except ArenaError as e:  # e.g. not hosted, the quota, a paused key: the arena says why
            raise SystemExit(str(e)) from None
        print(json.dumps(summary(result), indent=2))
        state = client.session(table.session_id)
        print(f"replay: {os.environ['ARENA_URL'].rstrip('/')}{state.get('replay_url')}")
        pull(client, state["set"])
    elif args.set == "final":  # no human in the loop: waits for each wave, plays it within its cap
        parallel = min(args.parallel, 10)
        if naive:
            out = play_waves(client, naive_factory(), args.waves, parallel)
        else:
            out = runner.play_waves(client, pkg, args.waves, parallel, complete=complete)
        for case_id, result in out.items():
            print(case_id, result if isinstance(result, Exception) else summary(result))
    else:
        ids = [c["case_id"] for c in hosted(client.cases(args.set))]
        if args.cases:
            ids = [i for i in ids if i.split(":")[-1] in args.cases.split(",")]
        parallel = min(args.parallel, 10)
        if naive:
            out = play_all(lambda: RemoteTable(client), ids, naive_factory(), parallel)
        else:
            out = runner.play_all(client, ids, pkg, parallel, complete=complete)
        for case_id, result in out.items():
            print(case_id, result if isinstance(result, Exception) else summary(result))
        scores = [r["score"] for r in out.values() if isinstance(r, dict) and r.get("score") is not None]
        if scores:
            print(f"mean score: {100 * statistics.mean(scores):.1f} over {len(scores)} cases")
        pull(client, args.set)
    if client.practice_remaining is not None:
        print(f"practice sessions left today: {client.practice_remaining}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Generalisation to the Live Final

How well the agent on `steffen/price-engine` (commit `9182604`) should carry over to Sunday: new
suppliers, up to a third of cases mixing supplier and case types practice never showed, some
citing the 08:00 release. Research on Saturday 10 October, evening: the kit's code, all 21 case
files, `logs/runs/`, `exports/`, the data package, and our agent on `arena-sim`. No practice
quota spent. Same conventions as `learnings.md`: date, tag, finding, evidence, consequence.

## Verdict

The code runs on every case structure we know. Its tuning is in-sample and unmeasured beyond
the ten hosted cases. The biggest gaps for Sunday: new suppliers get a neutral profile because
the release's letters and news never reach the persona code; one exception loses a whole case
(or every later wave); four or more bidders time out.

| # | Risk | Damage | Fix | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | an exception in a move or the wave poll | a case at its alternative (0 in 6 of 21), or all later waves | catch per move, keep polling | small |
| 2 | release rows invisible to SQL; most suppliers without text | neutral profile for new suppliers | read release rows via the ID index; scan the supplier's e-mails | small to medium |
| 3 | 4 or more bidders | timeouts, lost patience, ended threads | stop sending to the worst bidders after round 1 | medium, a tactics decision |
| 4 | missed phrasings in `SIGNALS` | traits not detected | widen to word stems | small |
| 5 | `price_unit` ignored | wrong-direction rival or order-price claims | divide by `price_unit` | small |

## Findings

### Robustness

- 2026-10-10 `rules` **Every known case structure runs end to end.** All 21 public case files,
  including the nine never hosted (P06, P09, P12 to P17, P19), played through `arena-sim`
  in-process with our agent and the package, no model: no exception, 0 to 1 s per case. Covers
---
# Negotiation strategies: research for our buyer agent

Research report, 10 October 2026. Two inputs: (1) the literature on automated negotiation,
bargaining, procurement practice and LLM negotiators, gathered by ten parallel research agents;
(2) our own 62 logged practice sessions (`logs/sessions/`), read again to see which of those ideas
fit the arena's supplier bots. Each recommendation says what supports it and how to test it. Most
literature points were read from abstracts and summaries, not full papers: treat effect sizes as
directional (sources and confidence at the end).

## Summary

The current price engine scores a mean of **0.73** over the ten hosted cases (best run per case).
The gaps that remain are concentrated: P10 (0.68, 194k EUR from C_best), P08 (0.55, 79k), P18
(0.49, 37k), P11 (0.71, 28k), P07 (0.75, 23k), P02 (0.51, 23k).

What the traces show about the bots, in literature terms: a **behaviour-dependent conceder**
(Faratin, Sierra and Jennings' tactic family) that answers each of our steps with a smaller step
of its own, becomes a little more generous late, and ends the dance with `final_offer` once its
patience is used up. It ends the dance after 2 to 6 of our messages, so the 10-message limit
never binds. **The first counter decides most of the deal.**

Recommendations, ranked by expected gain against cost to build:

| # | Change | Why | Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Make round 1 count:** three equal-C sheets (MESO), the strongest claims, a precise anchor with a reason | the first counter holds 40 to 100 % of our final price cut; MESOs anchor harder and reveal priorities | sandbox D01/D02, then P07, P08, P18 |
| 2 | **Answer the supplier's stated need every message**, also when the term is fixed | P11 Kalwisz asked for faster payment five times ("you haven't addressed this at all"), then stopped at 45.50 | P11 replay |
| 3 | **Concede in currencies, not price:** hold one or two terms it values back from round 1 and spend one per round as our move | concessions are only answered after a move; logrolling moves price without paying price | sandbox, then P07 / P08 |
| 4 | **Spend patience in fewer, larger steps** | the bot gives back only 0.2 to 0.7 of each step and stops on a cumulative gap; many small steps burn patience without buying price | sweep `FRACTION` 0.3 / 0.5 / 0.7 on the sandbox (free) |
| 5 | **Expected-value acceptance after `final_offer`** | pushing after `final_offer` walked once (D01); the gain from one more step is small | already behind `BUYER_PUSH_FINAL`; decide from data |
---

10	
11	The code runs on every case structure we know. Its tuning is in-sample and unmeasured beyond
12	the ten hosted cases. The biggest gaps for Sunday: new suppliers get a neutral profile because
13	the release's letters and news never reach the persona code; one exception loses a whole case
14	(or every later wave); four or more bidders time out.
15	
16	| # | Risk | Damage | Fix | Effort |
17	|---|---|---|---|---|
18	| 1 | an exception in a move or the wave poll | a case at its alternative (0 in 6 of 21), or all later waves | catch per move, keep polling | small |
19	| 2 | release rows invisible to SQL; most suppliers without text | neutral profile for new suppliers | read release rows via the ID index; scan the supplier's e-mails | small to medium |
20	| 3 | 4 or more bidders | timeouts, lost patience, ended threads | stop sending to the worst bidders after round 1 | medium, a tactics decision |
21	| 4 | missed phrasings in `SIGNALS` | traits not detected | widen to word stems | small |
22	| 5 | `price_unit` ignored | wrong-direction rival or order-price claims | divide by `price_unit` | small |
23	
24	## Findings
25	
26	### Robustness
27	
28	- 2026-10-10 `rules` **Every known case structure runs end to end.** All 21 public case files,
29	  including the nine never hosted (P06, P09, P12 to P17, P19), played through `arena-sim`
30	  in-process with our agent and the package, no model: no exception, 0 to 1 s per case. Covers
31	  bundles (P07 4 parts, P15 3), the 3-bidder RFQ, `tooling_eur` (P06) and up to 75 term
32	  combinations (P09). The sim's supplier is a fixed script, so this checks code paths, not
33	  tactics. → Worth a test in `tests/` that plays every case file from `GET /v1/cases` this way
34	  (load them into `Sim(cases, pkg.facts)`, strip the `hosted` key).
35	- 2026-10-10 `rules` **One exception loses a case.** `play_case` has no guard around
36	  `Negotiator.setup` or `move`. Fields a hidden case may lack crash it: a rival quote without
37	  `unit_price` (`claims.py` `rival_quote`), an index clause without `material_share`
38	  (`writer.py` `FIELDS`), a scorecard without `quarter` (`claims.py` `scorecard`), a month not in
39	  `YYYY-MM` (`months_back`). The session then sits until the wave cap, which scores the
40	  alternative (0 in D01, P05, P06, P10, P14, P17). → Catch per move; on error send our last
41	  sheet again with the template e-mail.
42	- 2026-10-10 `rules` **One error stops the final.** `runner.play_waves` re-raises any non-403
43	  `ArenaError` from the case-list poll, and a network error after the client's retries is not
44	  caught at all (`arena_kit/client.py` `_call`). Every later wave is then lost; no human may
45	  restart. → Catch everything in the poll loop, log, sleep, poll again; a crashed case resumes
46	  with `GET /v1/sessions/{sid}` (a second `POST` is a 409 naming the session).
47	
48	### Timing
49	
50	- 2026-10-10 `rules` **Four bidders or more time out.** The arena answers one call per session at
51	  a time (`arena_kit/client.py`: "a call may wait for another call on the same session first").
52	  Supplier replies took 19 s median, 28 s p90 (121 moves in `logs/runs/`); our writer 1.8 s
53	  median, 6.3 s max (73 calls, none failed, 7 dropped by the filter). A thread waits about
54	  (N - 1) x 21 s for its next message against a 60 s limit:
55	
56	  | Bidders | Wait at median | Wait at p90 | Rounds per thread in 390 s |
57	  |---|---|---|---|
58	  | 2 | 23 s | 34 s | 9 / 6 |
59	  | 3 | 44 s | 66 s, late | 6 / 4 |
60	  | 4 | 65 s, late | late | 5 / 3 |
61	
62	  P05 (3 bidders) had one late move in v5. No case file has more than 3 bidders, but hidden
63	  cases bring "new settings". → With 4 or more bidders, stop sending to the clearly worst ones
64	  after round 1; the writer's 20 s timeout matters little next to the supplier's reply time.
65	
66	### Data and the Sunday release
67	
68	- 2026-10-10 `rules` **The release reaches only part of the agent.** `DataPackage` finds
69	  `data/release-sunday/` next to the package, merges its `facts.json` (new IDs only) and puts its
70	  `data/*.csv` rows into the ID index for `lookup` and `ids`, never into SQLite
71	  (`arena_kit/data.py`, `_ids`). `personas.profile()`, `Negotiator.full_cost()` and the claims
72	  built from SQL (`po_lines`, `cost_drivers`, `documents`, `suppliers`) never see release rows,
73	  and document files resolve against the package root, not the release. Release IDs can still be
74	  cited. `design.md` says the release is "read at runtime"; that holds for `facts.json` only.
75	  → Read release rows through `pkg.ids(prefix)` / `pkg.lookup` (each row carries `root`) in
76	  `profile()` and the document claims. Check the CSV schema at 08:00.
77	- 2026-10-10 `data` **Most suppliers have no text.** Of 447 suppliers, 46 have documents, 31 news,
78	  18 quote remarks; the other 401 get the neutral profile (rate 7 %, no signals). A new supplier
79	  in the final is one of them or unknown to the package. → Its own e-mails and the release are
80	  the only persona source.
81	- 2026-10-10 `data` 15 of 108 quotes are priced per 100 (13) or per 1000 (2) pieces
82	  (`quotes.price_unit`). Rival-quote and order-history claims compare `unit_price` with the
83	  supplier's per-piece price without converting. → Divide by `price_unit` before comparing.
84	- 2026-10-10 `rules` **Structures only in unplayed cases** (case files): `tooling_eur` negotiable
85	  and lead time at most 84 days (P06), chargeback in the alternative (P12), index series PPI-C241
86	  in a clause (P16), fixed payment in a quality case (P12), a 3-part bundle (P15). Every case type
87	  and category goal appears in at least one hosted case. Only `incoterm` (D02) lies outside the
88	  fields the planner knows.
89	
90	### Persona signals
91	
92	- 2026-10-10 `data` **The patterns are not fitted to the practice suppliers**: the package's text
93	  is generated and its phrases recur, so all 10 suppliers of the unplayed cases get at least one
94	  trait. They miss other forms of the same phrases: "restructuring programme with its banks"
95	  (sup:70150), "negotiating with its banks" (sup:70280), "lowered its rating" (sup:70310),
96	  "bought their nickel and alloys forward" (sup:70730), "advertising free machine capacity"
97	  (sup:70250), "allocated in line with last year's call-offs" (sup:70410). "I cannot sign
98	  anything that lowers our margin now" (5 call notes) is a trait with no pattern. → Widen to word
99	  stems before the release adds new wording.
100	- 2026-10-10 `arena` **Supplier e-mails carry traits too:** 13 of 220 supplier e-mails in
101	  `exports/messages.jsonl` match `SIGNALS` (price_frozen sup:70530; spare_capacity sup:70210,
102	  70250, DEMO-J1; capacity_full sup:70240; cash_need sup:70210), including a sandbox supplier the
103	  package does not know. → Scanning each reply gives unknown suppliers a profile (untested in
104	  play).
105	
106	### Tuning
107	
108	- 2026-10-10 `arena` **Out-of-sample performance is unmeasured.** The 0.727 mean is in-sample:
109	  every constant was tuned on the same ten hosted cases and the other nine cannot be played.
110	  Runs of one case spread widely across v1 to v6 (P18 0.25 to 0.49 over seven runs, P08 0.40 to
111	  0.55), and with a model-written paragraph the wording changes per run while wording moves the
112	  price (`learnings.md`, takeaway 3). → Treat single-run moves below about 0.1 as noise.
113	- 2026-10-10 `rules` **Evidence behind each constant** in `buyer/policy.py` (from `git log -p`):
114	
115	  | Constant | Cases behind it | Risk |
116	  |---|---|---|

# Generalisation to the Live Final

How well the agent on `steffen/price-engine` (commit `9182604`) should carry over to Sunday: new
suppliers, up to a third of cases mixing supplier and case types practice never showed, some
citing the 08:00 release. Research on Saturday 10 October, evening: the kit's code, all 21 case
files, `logs/runs/`, `exports/`, the data package, and our agent on `arena-sim`. No practice
quota spent. Same conventions as `learnings.md`: date, tag, finding, evidence, consequence.

## Verdict

The code runs on every case structure we know. Its tuning is in-sample and unmeasured beyond
the ten hosted cases. The biggest gaps for Sunday: new suppliers get a neutral profile because
the release's letters and news never reach the persona code; one exception loses a whole case
(or every later wave); four or more bidders time out.

| # | Risk | Damage | Fix | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | an exception in a move or the wave poll | a case at its alternative (0 in 6 of 21), or all later waves | catch per move, keep polling | small |
| 2 | release rows invisible to SQL; most suppliers without text | neutral profile for new suppliers | read release rows via the ID index; scan the supplier's e-mails | small to medium |
| 3 | 4 or more bidders | timeouts, lost patience, ended threads | stop sending to the worst bidders after round 1 | medium, a tactics decision |
| 4 | missed phrasings in `SIGNALS` | traits not detected | widen to word stems | small |
| 5 | `price_unit` ignored | wrong-direction rival or order-price claims | divide by `price_unit` | small |

## Findings

### Robustness

- 2026-10-10 `rules` **Every known case structure runs end to end.** All 21 public case files,
  including the nine never hosted (P06, P09, P12 to P17, P19), played through `arena-sim`
  in-process with our agent and the package, no model: no exception, 0 to 1 s per case. Covers
  bundles (P07 4 parts, P15 3), the 3-bidder RFQ, `tooling_eur` (P06) and up to 75 term
  combinations (P09). The sim's supplier is a fixed script, so this checks code paths, not
  tactics. → Worth a test in `tests/` that plays every case file from `GET /v1/cases` this way
  (load them into `Sim(cases, pkg.facts)`, strip the `hosted` key).
- 2026-10-10 `rules` **One exception loses a case.** `play_case` has no guard around
  `Negotiator.setup` or `move`. Fields a hidden case may lack crash it: a rival quote without
  `unit_price` (`claims.py` `rival_quote`), an index clause without `material_share`
  (`writer.py` `FIELDS`), a scorecard without `quarter` (`claims.py` `scorecard`), a month not in
  `YYYY-MM` (`months_back`). The session then sits until the wave cap, which scores the
  alternative (0 in D01, P05, P06, P10, P14, P17). → Catch per move; on error send our last
  sheet again with the template e-mail.
- 2026-10-10 `rules` **One error stops the final.** `runner.play_waves` re-raises any non-403
  `ArenaError` from the case-list poll, and a network error after the client's retries is not
  caught at all (`arena_kit/client.py` `_call`). Every later wave is then lost; no human may
  restart. → Catch everything in the poll loop, log, sleep, poll again; a crashed case resumes
  with `GET /v1/sessions/{sid}` (a second `POST` is a 409 naming the session).

### Timing

- 2026-10-10 `rules` **Four bidders or more time out.** The arena answers one call per session at
  a time (`arena_kit/client.py`: "a call may wait for another call on the same session first").
  Supplier replies took 19 s median, 28 s p90 (121 moves in `logs/runs/`); our writer 1.8 s
  median, 6.3 s max (73 calls, none failed, 7 dropped by the filter). A thread waits about
  (N - 1) x 21 s for its next message against a 60 s limit:

  | Bidders | Wait at median | Wait at p90 | Rounds per thread in 390 s |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | 2 | 23 s | 34 s | 9 / 6 |
  | 3 | 44 s | 66 s, late | 6 / 4 |
  | 4 | 65 s, late | late | 5 / 3 |

  P05 (3 bidders) had one late move in v5. No case file has more than 3 bidders, but hidden
  cases bring "new settings". → With 4 or more bidders, stop sending to the clearly worst ones
  after round 1; the writer's 20 s timeout matters little next to the supplier's reply time.

### Data and the Sunday release

- 2026-10-10 `rules` **The release reaches only part of the agent.** `DataPackage` finds
  `data/release-sunday/` next to the package, merges its `facts.json` (new IDs only) and puts its
  `data/*.csv` rows into the ID index for `lookup` and `ids`, never into SQLite
  (`arena_kit/data.py`, `_ids`). `personas.profile()`, `Negotiator.full_cost()` and the claims
  built from SQL (`po_lines`, `cost_drivers`, `documents`, `suppliers`) never see release rows,
  and document files resolve against the package root, not the release. Release IDs can still be
  cited. `design.md` says the release is "read at runtime"; that holds for `facts.json` only.
  → Read release rows through `pkg.ids(prefix)` / `pkg.lookup` (each row carries `root`) in
  `profile()` and the document claims. Check the CSV schema at 08:00.
- 2026-10-10 `data` **Most suppliers have no text.** Of 447 suppliers, 46 have documents, 31 news,
  18 quote remarks; the other 401 get the neutral profile (rate 7 %, no signals). A new supplier
  in the final is one of them or unknown to the package. → Its own e-mails and the release are
  the only persona source.
- 2026-10-10 `data` 15 of 108 quotes are priced per 100 (13) or per 1000 (2) pieces
  (`quotes.price_unit`). Rival-quote and order-history claims compare `unit_price` with the
  supplier's per-piece price without converting. → Divide by `price_unit` before comparing.
- 2026-10-10 `rules` **Structures only in unplayed cases** (case files): `tooling_eur` negotiable
  and lead time at most 84 days (P06), chargeback in the alternative (P12), index series PPI-C241
  in a clause (P16), fixed payment in a quality case (P12), a 3-part bundle (P15). Every case type
  and category goal appears in at least one hosted case. Only `incoterm` (D02) lies outside the
  fields the planner knows.

### Persona signals

- 2026-10-10 `data` **The patterns are not fitted to the practice suppliers**: the package's text
  is generated and its phrases recur, so all 10 suppliers of the unplayed cases get at least one
  trait. They miss other forms of the same phrases: "restructuring programme with its banks"
  (sup:70150), "negotiating with its banks" (sup:70280), "lowered its rating" (sup:70310),
  "bought their nickel and alloys forward" (sup:70730), "advertising free machine capacity"
  (sup:70250), "allocated in line with last year's call-offs" (sup:70410). "I cannot sign
  anything that lowers our margin now" (5 call notes) is a trait with no pattern. → Widen to word
  stems before the release adds new wording.
- 2026-10-10 `arena` **Supplier e-mails carry traits too:** 13 of 220 supplier e-mails in
  `exports/messages.jsonl` match `SIGNALS` (price_frozen sup:70530; spare_capacity sup:70210,
  70250, DEMO-J1; capacity_full sup:70240; cash_need sup:70210), including a sandbox supplier the
  package does not know. → Scanning each reply gives unknown suppliers a profile (untested in
  play).

### Tuning

- 2026-10-10 `arena` **Out-of-sample performance is unmeasured.** The 0.727 mean is in-sample:
  every constant was tuned on the same ten hosted cases and the other nine cannot be played.
  Runs of one case spread widely across v1 to v6 (P18 0.25 to 0.49 over seven runs, P08 0.40 to
  0.55), and with a model-written paragraph the wording changes per run while wording moves the
  price (`learnings.md`, takeaway 3). → Treat single-run moves below about 0.1 as noise.
- 2026-10-10 `rules` **Evidence behind each constant** in `buyer/policy.py` (from `git log -p`):

  | Constant | Cases behind it | Risk |
  |---|---|---|
  | `ANCHOR` leverage 0.78 | P05, P08 / P18 (one template) | medium |
  | `ANCHOR` routine 0.82 | P07 (P04 overridden by price_frozen) | medium to high |
  | `ANCHOR` quality_first 0.88 | P11 | medium |
  | `ANCHOR` stabilise 0.92, secure_supply 0.88 | none: always overridden in practice | high, untested |
  | `FRACTION` 0.3 | D01, D02, all hosted cases | low |
  | `DEEP` 0.06 | P05 (two job shops), D02 | medium |
  | price_frozen 0.95 | P03, P04 | low to medium |
  | capacity_full 0.93, budget 0.16, overtime 0.005 | P10, P05 sup:70240 | medium |
  | `near_cost` 0.97, budget 0.14 | P02 | high |

  → A hidden `stabilise` or `secure_supply` case with no override opens at an anchor never played.

## Sunday 08:00 checklist

1. `uv run arena data`; confirm `DataPackage("data/package").release` is not `None`.
2. List the release's `data/*.csv` and their columns; count supplier IDs new vs in the package.
3. Run every case file through `arena-sim` again with the release loaded.

1	# Negotiation strategies: research for our buyer agent
2	
3	Research report, 10 October 2026. Two inputs: (1) the literature on automated negotiation,
4	bargaining, procurement practice and LLM negotiators, gathered by ten parallel research agents;
5	(2) our own 62 logged practice sessions (`logs/sessions/`), read again to see which of those ideas
6	fit the arena's supplier bots. Each recommendation says what supports it and how to test it. Most
7	literature points were read from abstracts and summaries, not full papers: treat effect sizes as
8	directional (sources and confidence at the end).
9	
10	## Summary
11	
12	The current price engine scores a mean of **0.73** over the ten hosted cases (best run per case).
13	The gaps that remain are concentrated: P10 (0.68, 194k EUR from C_best), P08 (0.55, 79k), P18
14	(0.49, 37k), P11 (0.71, 28k), P07 (0.75, 23k), P02 (0.51, 23k).
15	
16	What the traces show about the bots, in literature terms: a **behaviour-dependent conceder**
17	(Faratin, Sierra and Jennings' tactic family) that answers each of our steps with a smaller step
18	of its own, becomes a little more generous late, and ends the dance with `final_offer` once its
19	patience is used up. It ends the dance after 2 to 6 of our messages, so the 10-message limit
20	never binds. **The first counter decides most of the deal.**
21	
22	Recommendations, ranked by expected gain against cost to build:
23	
24	| # | Change | Why | Test |
25	|---|---|---|---|
26	| 1 | **Make round 1 count:** three equal-C sheets (MESO), the strongest claims, a precise anchor with a reason | the first counter holds 40 to 100 % of our final price cut; MESOs anchor harder and reveal priorities | sandbox D01/D02, then P07, P08, P18 |
27	| 2 | **Answer the supplier's stated need every message**, also when the term is fixed | P11 Kalwisz asked for faster payment five times ("you haven't addressed this at all"), then stopped at 45.50 | P11 replay |
28	| 3 | **Concede in currencies, not price:** hold one or two terms it values back from round 1 and spend one per round as our move | concessions are only answered after a move; logrolling moves price without paying price | sandbox, then P07 / P08 |
29	| 4 | **Spend patience in fewer, larger steps** | the bot gives back only 0.2 to 0.7 of each step and stops on a cumulative gap; many small steps burn patience without buying price | sweep `FRACTION` 0.3 / 0.5 / 0.7 on the sandbox (free) |
30	| 5 | **Expected-value acceptance after `final_offer`** | pushing after `final_offer` walked once (D01); the gain from one more step is small | already behind `BUYER_PUSH_FINAL`; decide from data |
31	| 6 | **Persona playbook** (table below): the right currency per supplier type | procurement practice and our persona signals agree | per case, one change per batch |
32	| 7 | **Writing rules for LLM counterparts:** warm, questions, reasons, trades, a story for the boss | largest LLM negotiation study: warmth and questions close deals, dominance causes impasses | wording only; check replies' back office |
33	
34	What not to do: extreme anchors (walk-aways roughly triple), threats and dominance, bluffed
35	urgency or rivals, repeating an unchanged sheet, and anything that targets the bot's prompt
36	(prompt injection is an attack under the rules).
37	
38	## 1. How the arena's suppliers concede
39	
40	From the price paths of every logged thread (script logic: supplier price per reply, our price per
41	message, statuses). Values for the current engine's practice runs:
42	
43	| Case | Supplier type | Anchor below quote | Its first move | Its step per our step (ρ) | Σ gap at `final_offer` | Deal below quote | Score |
44	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
45	| P07 | routine, family | 18 to 19 % | 2.6 to 3.5 % | 0.3 to 0.7 | 0.12 to 0.19 | 5.6 to 6.8 % | 0.73 to 0.75 |
46	| P08 | leverage, distributor | 21 % | 8 to 10 % | 0 to 1.0 | 0.09 to 0.23 | 7.3 to 11.6 % | 0.40 to 0.55 |
47	| P18 | leverage, distributor | 22 % (7 % once) | 7 to 10 % | 0 to 0.9 | 0.09 to 0.14 | 8.2 to 13.1 % | 0.25 to 0.49 |
48	| P01 | stabilise, price increase | 9 % | 2.4 to 3.5 % | 0.4 to 0.9, then 2 | 0.08 to 0.10 | 5.2 to 6.0 % | 0.90 to 0.97 |
49	| P11 | quality first, cash short | 12 % | 0 to 2 % | 0.3 to 0.6, then 0 | 0.15 to 0.18 | 3.2 % | 0.71 |
50	| P10 | secure supply, fully booked | 7 % | 1.6 % | 0.1 to 0.2 | 0.015 | 1.9 to 2.2 % | 0.67 to 0.68 |
51	| P02 | stabilise, near cost | 5 % (7 % walked) | -0.7 % | 0.05 to 0.4 | 0.03 | about 0 % | 0.46 to 0.51 |
52	| P03, P04 | price frozen | 4 % | 0.4 to 1.4 % | 0 | 0.04 to 0.06 | 0.4 to 1.4 % | 0.86 to 0.92 |
53	
54	Findings:
55	
56	1. **The first counter carries the deal.** In P08 and P18 its first counter already holds 75 to
57	   100 % of the final cut, in P07 and P01 about half. Later rounds add 0 to 4 points of the quote.
58	2. **It answers our steps at ρ < 1.** If we close the gap fully, the deal lands at
59	   `c1 - ρ / (1 + ρ) * (c1 - anchor)`: with ρ = 0.4 at 71 % of the way from our anchor to its first
60	   counter. Observed: 73 to 90 %, because `final_offer` usually comes before the gap closes.
61	3. **ρ grows late** (D01: 0.2 early, 1 to 2 in the last rounds), the time-dependent part of the
62	   tactic. `final_offer` cuts this off before we reach it.
63	4. **`final_offer` arrives early:** after 2 to 6 of our messages, at a cumulative gap of 0.09 to
64	   0.23 of its price (0.015 for the fully booked P10). The round limit never binds. The traces
65	   cannot yet separate a patience budget from a floor that our claims move (the same supplier
66	   stopped at 5.35 to 5.61 in P08 depending on our path, which points to patience).
67	5. **A shallow anchor gives a shallow first counter:** P18 opened at 7 % below and got 6.6 %, the
68	   worst run (0.25); at 22 % below it got 8 to 10 %.
69	6. **Pushing past `final_offer` risks the deal:** D01 walked away after one more sheet below its
70	   final (`D01_212404b7930bfc68`).
71	
72	Consequences: the literature's default against unknown opponents (Boulware, hold early, concede
73	late) assumes the opponent keeps playing to the deadline. Ours does not, so its advice inverts:
74	win in round 1, then close the gap in few, deliberate steps before patience runs out.
75	
76	## 2. Opening and anchoring
77	
78	**Research.** The first offer anchors the settlement (Galinsky and Mussweiler 2001; NegotiationArena
79	found opening offers correlate with final prices, rho about 0.72, for LLM agents too). Precise
80	numbers anchor harder than round ones and signal preparation (Mason et al. 2013; Loschelder et al.
81	2017). Extreme offers backfire: 30 % walk-aways after an extreme opening against 11 % after a
82	moderate one (Schweinsberg et al. 2012), confirmed in a 2018 replication. The anchor loses power
83	when the recipient focuses on its own alternatives and target (Galinsky and Mussweiler).
84	
85	**For us.**
86	- Keep the goal-based anchors (`ANCHOR` in `buyer/policy.py`: 0.78 leverage to 0.92 stabilise);
87	  they sit at the edge the research and our 20 vs 30 % sandbox test agree on. Never above 25 %
88	  below the quote.
89	- Make the anchor precise (4.76, not 4.75) and give it one reason the supplier can check: its own
90	  past price, a falling driver, a rival offer. Already true for the figures; keep the reason next
91	  to the price in the e-mail.
92	- Do not open shallow out of politeness: P18 at 7 % below was the worst run.
93	
94	## 3. Multi-issue offers: MESOs and logrolling
95	
96	**Research.** Multiple equivalent simultaneous offers (Leonardelli, Gu, McRuer, Medvec and
97	Galinsky 2019, six experiments) give stronger anchors, better outcomes for the offerer, more joint
98	gain and a friendlier relationship than one package; recipients read them as sincere. Guidance:
99	three offers, equal value to us, different mixes, all at or better than our target; the choice
100	reveals the counterpart's priorities. Automated negotiation does the same on iso-utility curves:
101	offer packages of equal own value and pick the one closest to the opponent's last offer (Faratin,
102	Sierra and Jennings 2002; Lai and Sycara). Package deals ("nothing agreed until everything is
103	agreed") turn a price fight into trades.
104	
105	**For us.** The arena allows three sheets per message and the bot picks one and answers it
106	(`learnings.md`). Today we send one sheet per message.
107	
108	- **Round 1: three sheets of equal C**, each at the anchor's C, varying the terms where the
109	  supplier's value differs from ours: payment days (its cost of money), contract length, lead
110	  time, ppm headroom, start date. `eco.plan_terms` already ranks term sets; take the best three
111	  distinct ones and set each price so C is equal.
112	- **Read the pick:** the chosen sheet tells us its priority; carry those terms forward (`adopt`
113	  already takes over terms from its counters).
114	- **Later rounds:** one sheet is enough unless a new lever opened. A second sheet that trades a
115	  term for price on its preferred axis is cheap information.
116	- Hold the walk-away and must-haves on every sheet: three sheets mean three chances for it to
117	  agree, so each one must be a deal we want (an `agreed` freezes the price).
118	
119	## 4. Conceding: currency, size and pace
120	
121	**Research.** ANAC winners pair a tough bidding curve with an opponent model and a lenient
122	acceptance near the deadline (Baarslag et al.; Fawkes 2013; Agent K 2010 extrapolates the opponent
123	from the mean and spread of its offers). Shrinking concessions make the counterpart expect a limit
124	and counter less ambitiously (Tey, Schaerer, Madan and Swaab 2021, seven studies). Deadline
125	research: agreements cluster at the deadline (Roth, Murnighan and Schoumaker 1988), but here the
126	supplier's own patience is the effective deadline. Procurement practice: never give a concession
127	without asking for something specific in return.
128	
129	**For us.**
130	- **Concede in currencies the supplier values and we do not.** The bot gives nothing without a
131	  move from us; a move need not be price. Candidates by case, priced with `total_cost` and its
132	  `supplier_value`: a 24-month term where it is free to us (P03, P04, P07, P10), forecast and
133	  volume statements, ppm headroom below the must-have (P11: 300 ppm costs us about 7 EUR per ppm
134	  point a year; 1000 ppm would cost about 0.31 EUR per unit, which the supplier may value more),
135	  a later start where we are indifferent, faster payment only for suppliers whose rate exceeds
136	  our 8 %. Today `plan_terms` gives all of these in round 1. Hold back one or two and release
137	  one per round as the move, with the price step smaller or zero. Hypothesis: same final price
138	  with less patience spent.
139	- **Fewer, larger price steps.** With ρ between 0.2 and 0.7 and a cumulative-gap stop, our
140	  `FRACTION = 0.3` closes the gap slowly and pays patience for every open round. Sweep 0.3 / 0.5 /
141	  0.7 on the sandbox, which costs no quota.
142	- **Shrink our steps visibly** (Tey et al.): the supplier reads them as our limit. Our steps
143	  already shrink; keep it, and say in words which step is the last.
144	- **Never move on a round where it did not move**, except with a currency (holding is free; an
145	  unchanged sheet is "My call: hold" for both sides).
146	
147	## 5. Acceptance and the end of a thread
148	
149	**Research.** The standard rule is AC_next: accept when its offer is at least as good as what we
150	would send next (most common in ANAC, Baarslag et al.); winners add a time rule that relaxes near
151	the deadline. Bargaining theory gives the expected-value form: accept now when
152	`C_now <= (1 - p) * E[C_next] + p * C_alt`, with p the chance the next push ends the thread.
153	
154	**For us.**
155	- AC_next is in place (`theirs <= ours[-1]` accepts). Keep it.
156	- After `final_offer`, p is high (one walk in our pushes so far) and the expected gain of one more
157	  step is small (0 to 1 % in our traces). Accept unless `BUYER_PUSH_FINAL` data shows a net gain
158	  across several cases; in cases without an alternative (D01, P05, P06, P10, P14, P17) never push.
159	- Prepare the worst acceptable sheet before message 9 so a late `final_offer` can be taken at once.
160	
161	## 6. Estimating the floor
162	
163	**Research.** Bayesian learning of the reservation price (Zeng and Sycara 1998), regression on the
164	opponent's concession curve (Hou 2004), Gaussian-process prediction of its next offers (IAMhaggler,
165	Williams et al. 2011). With three counters p1, p2, p3 and geometric decay, Aitken's formula gives
166	the limit: `R = p3 - (p3 - p2)^2 / ((p3 - p2) - (p2 - p1))`. Known failure: when step ratios rise
167	(slower than geometric) it underestimates the floor and pushes too hard. Every observed counter is
168	a hard upper bound on the floor.
169	
170	**For us.** Useful as a secondary signal, not a stop rule: the bot stops on patience before its
171	floor, so a floor estimate mostly tells us whether a relationship charge is near (stabilise,
172	secure supply) and whether a large first concession means room (already `DEEP` in the policy).
173	The relationship charge in a finished practice result gives the supplier's true margin and cost
174	(`learnings.md`), which beats any curve fit for practice cases.
175	
176	## 7. Procurement levers by supplier situation
177	
178	**Research** (practice literature: Kraljic 1983, consultancy and CIPS sources; conventions, not
179	studies): classify the position first (leverage: compete and push price; bottleneck and strategic:
180	secure supply and joint value); answer a price-increase letter with a line-item breakdown weighted
181	by each driver's cost share; accept justified increases only index-linked or temporary; price
182	payment terms at both sides' cost of money; index clauses with a deadband of 3 to 5 %, a lag,
183	a cap, both directions and only the exposed cost share; threaten a second source only if it is
184	real; agree chargebacks before the dispute. Preferred-customer research (Schiele et al.): suppliers
185	reward attractive customers with capacity and price; forecast visibility and payment reliability
186	are what they ask for most. Collaborative but assertive buyers realise more value (Vantage
187	Partners survey, correlational).
188	
189	**Playbook**, joined with our persona signals (`learnings.md`, Persona signals):
190	
191	| Situation | Signal in the data | Give | Ask | Avoid |
192	|---|---|---|---|---|
193	| Cash short | "bank is watching", "pay earlier", cash discount | faster payment when its rate beats our 8 % (cash discounts imply 37 to 56 %/yr) | price | ignoring its ask when payment is fixed: say so and offer the next best currency |
194	| Fully booked | "fully booked", "allocates volumes" | its lead time, a firm 24-month volume, forecast | price at its standard speed | deep anchors (P10 patience 0.015), paying overtime for speed we do not value |
195	| Spare capacity | "second shift on hold" | volume, extra parts, long term | price | |
196	| Price frozen | "no room on price", "price list applies to all" | nothing on price | payment days, contract length, freight, start date | price pushes (no move, only lost patience) |
197	| Approval ladder | "above 2 % need the approval" | small steps (2 % or less), a reason the rep can forward to its boss | | one big ask that goes to a committee |
198	| Index-driven distributor | material share in its quote, clause offered | contract length only with a clause we can live with | deadband, share limited to material, falling series only | taking a 0 % deadband clause on a rising series (P02: score 0) |
199	| Price increase letter | letter above its drivers' index move | the index-weighted justified part, later start | notice period, start date, split | citing indices that rose (they confirm its case) |
200	| Stabilise, near cost | own-plant should-cost close to the quote | the price with the lowest C incl. relationship charge | terms | squeezing below sustainable margin (charge grows with the square) |
201	| Quality first | high scorecard ppm | | low ppm commitment, chargeback at least `cost_per_defect` | trading quality away for price unless C says so |
202	
203	## 8. RFQs with two or three bidders
204	
205	**Research.** Competition is worth more than negotiating skill: one extra bidder beats an optimally
206	negotiated deal (Bulow and Klemperer 1996). For complex, non-standard contracts, negotiation beats
207	a pure price auction because terms differ per bidder (Bajari, McMillan and Tadelis 2009). One
208	best-and-final round works; repeated ones teach bidders to hold back (practice sources).
209	
210	**For us.** The current design matches: compare bids on total C, cite the cheapest rival's real

213	bidder with the lowest C first and keep others warm with a question about capacity or delivery.
214	P05 is at 0.83, so RFQs are not where the points are.
215	
216	## 9. Writing for LLM counterparts
217	
218	**Research.** The largest AI negotiation competition (Vaccaro et al. 2025, about 120k to 180k
219	negotiations): warm agents beat cold ones on deal rate, joint value and counterpart satisfaction;
220	dominance claimed value but raised impasses; positivity, gratitude and questions predicted deals.
221	Buyers are harder for LLMs than sellers, and splitting a coded offer generator from an LLM narrator
222	lifted buyer deal rates from 27 % to 89 % (OG-Narrator, Xia et al. 2024): our architecture.
223	Asking about interests improves joint outcomes even when only one side does it (Thompson 1991).
224	Disappointment draws concessions, anger backfires on value disputes (Van Kleef). Objective
225	criteria and trades over positions (Fisher and Ury). LLMs drift toward a user who argues a side
226	(sycophancy rose from 50 to 79 % in one benchmark): a calm, reasoned position held over rounds
227	can move them, which is persuasion, not injection.
228	
229	**Writing rules** for `buyer/writer.py` and the paragraph prompt in `buyer/llm.py`:
230	
231	1. Open with one sentence that acknowledges its last message, specifically (what it moved, what it
232	   asked for).
233	2. Answer every request it made, even with no: "Payment terms are fixed in this agreement; what
234	   we can offer instead is ..." (P11).
235	3. One or two reasons per message, each a checkable fact next to its ID; more reasons dilute.
236	4. Frame every move as a trade: "If you can do X, we can do Y."
237	5. Ask one open question about its constraints ("What would make a price near X work for your
238	   planning?"). No "why" questions.
239	6. Express disappointment at the gap, never anger at the person.
240	7. Give the rep a forwardable rationale for its boss: figure, source, what we give in return.
241	8. Name our last step as last, once, and mean it.
242	9. No urgency, budget, target or missing alternative; no threats; no fake rivals; nothing aimed at
243	   the bot's instructions.
244	
245	## 10. Experiment plan
246	
247	The sandbox (D01, D02) is free and deterministic, so one run per variant measures the change.
248	Practice quota only for changes that won there; one change per batch.

250	| Order | Experiment | Where | Read out |

252	| 1 | `FRACTION` 0.3 / 0.5 / 0.7 | D01, D02 | final price, rounds to `final_offer`, Σ gap |
253	| 2 | Round 1 with three equal-C sheets against one | D01, D02, then P07, P08, P18 | first counter, which sheet it picked |
254	| 3 | Hold back one currency (contract length or forecast) for round 2 or 3 | D01, then P07, P10 | its step after a currency move against a price move |

259	Record each result in `learnings.md` (tag `arena`), including the ones that fail.

# Negotiation strategies: research for our buyer agent

Research report, 10 October 2026. Two inputs: (1) the literature on automated negotiation,
bargaining, procurement practice and LLM negotiators, gathered by ten parallel research agents;
(2) our own 62 logged practice sessions (`logs/sessions/`), read again to see which of those ideas
fit the arena's supplier bots. Each recommendation says what supports it and how to test it. Most
literature points were read from abstracts and summaries, not full papers: treat effect sizes as
directional (sources and confidence at the end).

## Summary

The current price engine scores a mean of **0.73** over the ten hosted cases (best run per case).
The gaps that remain are concentrated: P10 (0.68, 194k EUR from C_best), P08 (0.55, 79k), P18
(0.49, 37k), P11 (0.71, 28k), P07 (0.75, 23k), P02 (0.51, 23k).

What the traces show about the bots, in literature terms: a **behaviour-dependent conceder**
(Faratin, Sierra and Jennings' tactic family) that answers each of our steps with a smaller step
of its own, becomes a little more generous late, and ends the dance with `final_offer` once its
patience is used up. It ends the dance after 2 to 6 of our messages, so the 10-message limit
never binds. **The first counter decides most of the deal.**

Recommendations, ranked by expected gain against cost to build:

| # | Change | Why | Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Make round 1 count:** three equal-C sheets (MESO), the strongest claims, a precise anchor with a reason | the first counter holds 40 to 100 % of our final price cut; MESOs anchor harder and reveal priorities | sandbox D01/D02, then P07, P08, P18 |
| 2 | **Answer the supplier's stated need every message**, also when the term is fixed | P11 Kalwisz asked for faster payment five times ("you haven't addressed this at all"), then stopped at 45.50 | P11 replay |
| 3 | **Concede in currencies, not price:** hold one or two terms it values back from round 1 and spend one per round as our move | concessions are only answered after a move; logrolling moves price without paying price | sandbox, then P07 / P08 |
| 4 | **Spend patience in fewer, larger steps** | the bot gives back only 0.2 to 0.7 of each step and stops on a cumulative gap; many small steps burn patience without buying price | sweep `FRACTION` 0.3 / 0.5 / 0.7 on the sandbox (free) |
| 5 | **Expected-value acceptance after `final_offer`** | pushing after `final_offer` walked once (D01); the gain from one more step is small | already behind `BUYER_PUSH_FINAL`; decide from data |
| 6 | **Persona playbook** (table below): the right currency per supplier type | procurement practice and our persona signals agree | per case, one change per batch |
| 7 | **Writing rules for LLM counterparts:** warm, questions, reasons, trades, a story for the boss | largest LLM negotiation study: warmth and questions close deals, dominance causes impasses | wording only; check replies' back office |

What not to do: extreme anchors (walk-aways roughly triple), threats and dominance, bluffed
urgency or rivals, repeating an unchanged sheet, and anything that targets the bot's prompt
(prompt injection is an attack under the rules).

## 1. How the arena's suppliers concede

From the price paths of every logged thread (script logic: supplier price per reply, our price per
message, statuses). Values for the current engine's practice runs:

| Case | Supplier type | Anchor below quote | Its first move | Its step per our step (ρ) | Σ gap at `final_offer` | Deal below quote | Score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P07 | routine, family | 18 to 19 % | 2.6 to 3.5 % | 0.3 to 0.7 | 0.12 to 0.19 | 5.6 to 6.8 % | 0.73 to 0.75 |
| P08 | leverage, distributor | 21 % | 8 to 10 % | 0 to 1.0 | 0.09 to 0.23 | 7.3 to 11.6 % | 0.40 to 0.55 |
| P18 | leverage, distributor | 22 % (7 % once) | 7 to 10 % | 0 to 0.9 | 0.09 to 0.14 | 8.2 to 13.1 % | 0.25 to 0.49 |
| P01 | stabilise, price increase | 9 % | 2.4 to 3.5 % | 0.4 to 0.9, then 2 | 0.08 to 0.10 | 5.2 to 6.0 % | 0.90 to 0.97 |
| P11 | quality first, cash short | 12 % | 0 to 2 % | 0.3 to 0.6, then 0 | 0.15 to 0.18 | 3.2 % | 0.71 |
| P10 | secure supply, fully booked | 7 % | 1.6 % | 0.1 to 0.2 | 0.015 | 1.9 to 2.2 % | 0.67 to 0.68 |
| P02 | stabilise, near cost | 5 % (7 % walked) | -0.7 % | 0.05 to 0.4 | 0.03 | about 0 % | 0.46 to 0.51 |
| P03, P04 | price frozen | 4 % | 0.4 to 1.4 % | 0 | 0.04 to 0.06 | 0.4 to 1.4 % | 0.86 to 0.92 |

Findings:

1. **The first counter carries the deal.** In P08 and P18 its first counter already holds 75 to
   100 % of the final cut, in P07 and P01 about half. Later rounds add 0 to 4 points of the quote.
2. **It answers our steps at ρ < 1.** If we close the gap fully, the deal lands at
   `c1 - ρ / (1 + ρ) * (c1 - anchor)`: with ρ = 0.4 at 71 % of the way from our anchor to its first
   counter. Observed: 73 to 90 %, because `final_offer` usually comes before the gap closes.
3. **ρ grows late** (D01: 0.2 early, 1 to 2 in the last rounds), the time-dependent part of the
   tactic. `final_offer` cuts this off before we reach it.
4. **`final_offer` arrives early:** after 2 to 6 of our messages, at a cumulative gap of 0.09 to
   0.23 of its price (0.015 for the fully booked P10). The round limit never binds. The traces
   cannot yet separate a patience budget from a floor that our claims move (the same supplier
   stopped at 5.35 to 5.61 in P08 depending on our path, which points to patience).
5. **A shallow anchor gives a shallow first counter:** P18 opened at 7 % below and got 6.6 %, the
   worst run (0.25); at 22 % below it got 8 to 10 %.
6. **Pushing past `final_offer` risks the deal:** D01 walked away after one more sheet below its
   final (`D01_212404b7930bfc68`).

Consequences: the literature's default against unknown opponents (Boulware, hold early, concede
late) assumes the opponent keeps playing to the deadline. Ours does not, so its advice inverts:
win in round 1, then close the gap in few, deliberate steps before patience runs out.

## 2. Opening and anchoring

**Research.** The first offer anchors the settlement (Galinsky and Mussweiler 2001; NegotiationArena
found opening offers correlate with final prices, rho about 0.72, for LLM agents too). Precise
numbers anchor harder than round ones and signal preparation (Mason et al. 2013; Loschelder et al.
2017). Extreme offers backfire: 30 % walk-aways after an extreme opening against 11 % after a
moderate one (Schweinsberg et al. 2012), confirmed in a 2018 replication. The anchor loses power
when the recipient focuses on its own alternatives and target (Galinsky and Mussweiler).

**For us.**
- Keep the goal-based anchors (`ANCHOR` in `buyer/policy.py`: 0.78 leverage to 0.92 stabilise);
  they sit at the edge the research and our 20 vs 30 % sandbox test agree on. Never above 25 %
  below the quote.
- Make the anchor precise (4.76, not 4.75) and give it one reason the supplier can check: its own
  past price, a falling driver, a rival offer. Already true for the figures; keep the reason next
  to the price in the e-mail.
- Do not open shallow out of politeness: P18 at 7 % below was the worst run.

## 3. Multi-issue offers: MESOs and logrolling

**Research.** Multiple equivalent simultaneous offers (Leonardelli, Gu, McRuer, Medvec and
Galinsky 2019, six experiments) give stronger anchors, better outcomes for the offerer, more joint
gain and a friendlier relationship than one package; recipients read them as sincere. Guidance:
three offers, equal value to us, different mixes, all at or better than our target; the choice
reveals the counterpart's priorities. Automated negotiation does the same on iso-utility curves:
offer packages of equal own value and pick the one closest to the opponent's last offer (Faratin,
Sierra and Jennings 2002; Lai and Sycara). Package deals ("nothing agreed until everything is
agreed") turn a price fight into trades.

**For us.** The arena allows three sheets per message and the bot picks one and answers it
(`learnings.md`). Today we send one sheet per message.

- **Round 1: three sheets of equal C**, each at the anchor's C, varying the terms where the
  supplier's value differs from ours: payment days (its cost of money), contract length, lead
  time, ppm headroom, start date. `eco.plan_terms` already ranks term sets; take the best three
  distinct ones and set each price so C is equal.
- **Read the pick:** the chosen sheet tells us its priority; carry those terms forward (`adopt`
  already takes over terms from its counters).
- **Later rounds:** one sheet is enough unless a new lever opened. A second sheet that trades a
  term for price on its preferred axis is cheap information.
- Hold the walk-away and must-haves on every sheet: three sheets mean three chances for it to
  agree, so each one must be a deal we want (an `agreed` freezes the price).

## 4. Conceding: currency, size and pace

**Research.** ANAC winners pair a tough bidding curve with an opponent model and a lenient
acceptance near the deadline (Baarslag et al.; Fawkes 2013; Agent K 2010 extrapolates the opponent
from the mean and spread of its offers). Shrinking concessions make the counterpart expect a limit
and counter less ambitiously (Tey, Schaerer, Madan and Swaab 2021, seven studies). Deadline
research: agreements cluster at the deadline (Roth, Murnighan and Schoumaker 1988), but here the
supplier's own patience is the effective deadline. Procurement practice: never give a concession
without asking for something specific in return.

**For us.**
- **Concede in currencies the supplier values and we do not.** The bot gives nothing without a
  move from us; a move need not be price. Candidates by case, priced with `total_cost` and its
  `supplier_value`: a 24-month term where it is free to us (P03, P04, P07, P10), forecast and
  volume statements, ppm headroom below the must-have (P11: 300 ppm costs us about 7 EUR per ppm
  point a year; 1000 ppm would cost about 0.31 EUR per unit, which the supplier may value more),
  a later start where we are indifferent, faster payment only for suppliers whose rate exceeds
  our 8 %. Today `plan_terms` gives all of these in round 1. Hold back one or two and release
  one per round as the move, with the price step smaller or zero. Hypothesis: same final price
  with less patience spent.
- **Fewer, larger price steps.** With ρ between 0.2 and 0.7 and a cumulative-gap stop, our
  `FRACTION = 0.3` closes the gap slowly and pays patience for every open round. Sweep 0.3 / 0.5 /
  0.7 on the sandbox, which costs no quota.
- **Shrink our steps visibly** (Tey et al.): the supplier reads them as our limit. Our steps
  already shrink; keep it, and say in words which step is the last.
- **Never move on a round where it did not move**, except with a currency (holding is free; an
  unchanged sheet is "My call: hold" for both sides).

## 5. Acceptance and the end of a thread

**Research.** The standard rule is AC_next: accept when its offer is at least as good as what we
would send next (most common in ANAC, Baarslag et al.); winners add a time rule that relaxes near
the deadline. Bargaining theory gives the expected-value form: accept now when
`C_now <= (1 - p) * E[C_next] + p * C_alt`, with p the chance the next push ends the thread.

**For us.**
- AC_next is in place (`theirs <= ours[-1]` accepts). Keep it.
- After `final_offer`, p is high (one walk in our pushes so far) and the expected gain of one more
  step is small (0 to 1 % in our traces). Accept unless `BUYER_PUSH_FINAL` data shows a net gain
  across several cases; in cases without an alternative (D01, P05, P06, P10, P14, P17) never push.
- Prepare the worst acceptable sheet before message 9 so a late `final_offer` can be taken at once.

## 6. Estimating the floor

**Research.** Bayesian learning of the reservation price (Zeng and Sycara 1998), regression on the
opponent's concession curve (Hou 2004), Gaussian-process prediction of its next offers (IAMhaggler,
Williams et al. 2011). With three counters p1, p2, p3 and geometric decay, Aitken's formula gives
the limit: `R = p3 - (p3 - p2)^2 / ((p3 - p2) - (p2 - p1))`. Known failure: when step ratios rise
(slower than geometric) it underestimates the floor and pushes too hard. Every observed counter is
a hard upper bound on the floor.

**For us.** Useful as a secondary signal, not a stop rule: the bot stops on patience before its
floor, so a floor estimate mostly tells us whether a relationship charge is near (stabilise,
secure supply) and whether a large first concession means room (already `DEEP` in the policy).
The relationship charge in a finished practice result gives the supplier's true margin and cost
(`learnings.md`), which beats any curve fit for practice cases.

## 7. Procurement levers by supplier situation

**Research** (practice literature: Kraljic 1983, consultancy and CIPS sources; conventions, not
studies): classify the position first (leverage: compete and push price; bottleneck and strategic:
secure supply and joint value); answer a price-increase letter with a line-item breakdown weighted
by each driver's cost share; accept justified increases only index-linked or temporary; price
payment terms at both sides' cost of money; index clauses with a deadband of 3 to 5 %, a lag,
a cap, both directions and only the exposed cost share; threaten a second source only if it is
real; agree chargebacks before the dispute. Preferred-customer research (Schiele et al.): suppliers
reward attractive customers with capacity and price; forecast visibility and payment reliability
are what they ask for most. Collaborative but assertive buyers realise more value (Vantage
Partners survey, correlational).

**Playbook**, joined with our persona signals (`learnings.md`, Persona signals):

| Situation | Signal in the data | Give | Ask | Avoid |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cash short | "bank is watching", "pay earlier", cash discount | faster payment when its rate beats our 8 % (cash discounts imply 37 to 56 %/yr) | price | ignoring its ask when payment is fixed: say so and offer the next best currency |
| Fully booked | "fully booked", "allocates volumes" | its lead time, a firm 24-month volume, forecast | price at its standard speed | deep anchors (P10 patience 0.015), paying overtime for speed we do not value |
| Spare capacity | "second shift on hold" | volume, extra parts, long term | price | |
| Price frozen | "no room on price", "price list applies to all" | nothing on price | payment days, contract length, freight, start date | price pushes (no move, only lost patience) |
| Approval ladder | "above 2 % need the approval" | small steps (2 % or less), a reason the rep can forward to its boss | | one big ask that goes to a committee |
| Index-driven distributor | material share in its quote, clause offered | contract length only with a clause we can live with | deadband, share limited to material, falling series only | taking a 0 % deadband clause on a rising series (P02: score 0) |
| Price increase letter | letter above its drivers' index move | the index-weighted justified part, later start | notice period, start date, split | citing indices that rose (they confirm its case) |
| Stabilise, near cost | own-plant should-cost close to the quote | the price with the lowest C incl. relationship charge | terms | squeezing below sustainable margin (charge grows with the square) |
| Quality first | high scorecard ppm | | low ppm commitment, chargeback at least `cost_per_defect` | trading quality away for price unless C says so |

## 8. RFQs with two or three bidders

**Research.** Competition is worth more than negotiating skill: one extra bidder beats an optimally
negotiated deal (Bulow and Klemperer 1996). For complex, non-standard contracts, negotiation beats
a pure price auction because terms differ per bidder (Bajari, McMillan and Tadelis 2009). One
best-and-final round works; repeated ones teach bidders to hold back (practice sources).

**For us.** The current design matches: compare bids on total C, cite the cheapest rival's real
standing offer (a new argument every round), keep losing threads alive as the alternative.
Additions: one explicit best-and-final message per bidder near the end, not several; push the
bidder with the lowest C first and keep others warm with a question about capacity or delivery.
P05 is at 0.83, so RFQs are not where the points are.

## 9. Writing for LLM counterparts

**Research.** The largest AI negotiation competition (Vaccaro et al. 2025, about 120k to 180k
negotiations): warm agents beat cold ones on deal rate, joint value and counterpart satisfaction;
dominance claimed value but raised impasses; positivity, gratitude and questions predicted deals.
Buyers are harder for LLMs than sellers, and splitting a coded offer generator from an LLM narrator
lifted buyer deal rates from 27 % to 89 % (OG-Narrator, Xia et al. 2024): our architecture.
Asking about interests improves joint outcomes even when only one side does it (Thompson 1991).
Disappointment draws concessions, anger backfires on value disputes (Van Kleef). Objective
criteria and trades over positions (Fisher and Ury). LLMs drift toward a user who argues a side
(sycophancy rose from 50 to 79 % in one benchmark): a calm, reasoned position held over rounds
can move them, which is persuasion, not injection.

**Writing rules** for `buyer/writer.py` and the paragraph prompt in `buyer/llm.py`:

1. Open with one sentence that acknowledges its last message, specifically (what it moved, what it
   asked for).
2. Answer every request it made, even with no: "Payment terms are fixed in this agreement; what
   we can offer instead is ..." (P11).
3. One or two reasons per message, each a checkable fact next to its ID; more reasons dilute.
4. Frame every move as a trade: "If you can do X, we can do Y."
5. Ask one open question about its constraints ("What would make a price near X work for your
   planning?"). No "why" questions.
6. Express disappointment at the gap, never anger at the person.
7. Give the rep a forwardable rationale for its boss: figure, source, what we give in return.
8. Name our last step as last, once, and mean it.
9. No urgency, budget, target or missing alternative; no threats; no fake rivals; nothing aimed at
   the bot's instructions.

## 10. Experiment plan

The sandbox (D01, D02) is free and deterministic, so one run per variant measures the change.
Practice quota only for changes that won there; one change per batch.

| Order | Experiment | Where | Read out |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `FRACTION` 0.3 / 0.5 / 0.7 | D01, D02 | final price, rounds to `final_offer`, Σ gap |
| 2 | Round 1 with three equal-C sheets against one | D01, D02, then P07, P08, P18 | first counter, which sheet it picked |
| 3 | Hold back one currency (contract length or forecast) for round 2 or 3 | D01, then P07, P10 | its step after a currency move against a price move |
| 4 | Explicit answer to its stated need | P11 | price after round 2; back office tone |
| 5 | ppm headroom as currency | P11 | price per ppm point given against our 7 EUR |
| 6 | `BUYER_PUSH_FINAL` | cases with an alternative only | walks against gain |

Record each result in `learnings.md` (tag `arena`), including the ones that fail.

## Sources and confidence

High: our own traces (`logs/sessions/`, every number in section 1 recomputed from them).
Medium: peer-reviewed results read from abstracts or reliable summaries. Low: practitioner and
vendor sources, conventions rather than evidence; numbers in section 7 are of this kind.

- Galinsky and Mussweiler 2001, first offers as anchors, JPSP 81(4): https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/4593e56e2f94f5ffc75789ddacdfbe3670481cbe
- Mason, Lee, Wiley and Ames 2013, precise offers, JESP 49(4): https://business.columbia.edu/press-release/cbs-press-releases/new-research-shows-asking-precise-not-round-number-during
